messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time

Vignette:
Eleanor has come to believe her world ended six months ago, on a rainy Tuesday evening at a downtown gallery opening. Before that night, her life at seventy-three, though quiet since her husband's passing, had a rhythm she cherished: the morning light in her studio, the familiar weight of a brush in her hand, the weekly visits from her son and his children. The disaster was a sudden, violent tearing of that fabric. One moment she was admiring a young artist's sculpture, the smell of cheap chardonnay hanging in the air; the next, a sound like thunder cracked directly overhead. The floor gave way in a roar of splintering wood and shattering glass. She remembers not a continuous event, but a series of stark, silent photographs in her mind: the terrified face of the young woman beside her, a cascade of plaster dust catching the light, her own hand pinned beneath a heavy beam. She was trapped for two hours, listening to the muffled sounds of crying from somewhere in the darkness, the scent of spilled wine and dust thick in her throat. The young woman she had been speaking with did not survive.

In the weeks that followed, Eleanor’s home, once her sanctuary, became a fortress. She stopped sleeping through the night, lying rigid in bed for hours, convinced that every creak of the old house was the groan of failing joists. She found herself listening intently for any sound that might signal an intruder, a new threat coming from the dark. The world outside felt menacing and unpredictable; her long-held belief that life was fundamentally fair and orderly had been completely destroyed. She retreated to her studio, throwing herself into her work with a frantic energy she hadn't felt in years. She would paint for ten hours straight, not from inspiration, but from a desperate need to keep her mind occupied, to build a wall of concentration so thick that no thoughts of the gallery could penetrate it.

The intrusions, however, found their way in. A memory would surface without warning, and as the mental snapshot of the wreckage appeared, she would feel an intense, nauseating wave of guilt. Why her and not the young artist? When the image of being trapped flashed in her mind, her body would betray her, her right arm and shoulder seizing up, contorting into the same painful position she had been held in by the debris. These moments were unbearable, and she learned quickly what to avoid. When a news report mentioned a structural collapse in another city, she would lunge for the remote. She tried with all her might to suppress any thought of the trauma, pushing it down whenever it surfaced. Her relationships began to fray under the strain. She cancelled a visit with her granddaughter, unable to face the possibility of the little girl crying over a scraped knee, as the sound had become inextricably linked to the suffering in the darkness. When her son brought over a bottle of wine for dinner, the smell of it uncorked in her kitchen sent a jolt of panic through her, and she lashed out with a fury that stunned them both. He left early, the bottle untouched on the counter.

Now, Eleanor spends most of her days alone in her studio, surrounded by canvases she no longer feels any connection to. The joy is gone, replaced by a hollow ache. She has come to believe that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again, that the part of her capable of happiness or peace was crushed in the rubble. The thought that her life is not worth living anymore has begun to feel less like a dramatic fear and more like a simple fact. It was her son’s tearful phone call last week that finally prompted her to seek help. He told her he missed his mother, that his children were afraid of her irritability. What frightened Eleanor most was not the memory of the collapse, but the realization that in her struggle to survive it, she was systematically destroying every beautiful thing she had left.
